question: Can every proper scoring rule induce a principled probability-pooling operator that is simultaneously max-min optimal, compatible with online weight learning, and characterized by natural aggregation axioms?

key_findings.claim: Quasi-arithmetic pooling averages forecasts in the exposure, or dual, space of a proper scoring rule.
key_findings.evidence: Definition 3.6 defines the unique p* whose scoring-rule exposure is the weighted expert exposure, interpreted through a subgradient when necessary. Equivalently, p* minimizes the weighted sum of Bregman divergences from p* to the expert reports, and it remains inside the scoring rule's finite forecast domain.

key_findings.claim: Familiar pools arise as scoring-rule-specific cases rather than universally appropriate aggregators.
key_findings.evidence: For the quadratic score, the exposure map is affine and QA pooling becomes the weighted linear pool. For the logarithmic score, averaging exposure corresponds to normalized weighted geometric probabilities, yielding logarithmic pooling.

anchors.section: 1.2 Quadratic scoring rule and linear pooling
Logarithmic scoring rule and logarithmic pooling

key_findings.claim: The QA report uniquely maximizes the subcontracting forecaster's worst-case profit over outcomes.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.1 considers an agent paid by score s while paying expert i the fraction wi of that expert's score. Reporting the QA pool uniquely maximizes minimum profit; the guaranteed profit is equal on every outcome receiving positive pooled probability, nonnegative, and strictly positive unless all positively weighted forecasts agree.

anchors.section: 4 QA pooling as a max-min optimal method / Theorem 4.1

key_findings.claim: Under convex exposure, the realized QA-pool score is concave in expert weights and supports adversarial no-regret learning against the best fixed pool.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5.1 proves outcome-wise concavity in the weights. For a bounded proper scoring rule with convex exposure, Theorem 5.3 applies online gradient descent and bounds regret by 3 sqrt(m) M sqrt(T), where M bounds the exposure norm, against the best fixed weighted QA pool in hindsight rather than merely the best single expert.

anchors.section: 5 Convex losses and learning expert weights / Theorem 5.1

key_findings.claim: In the binary case, a natural set of weighted-pooling axioms characterizes exactly the QA family.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 6.6 uses weight additivity, commutativity, associativity, continuity, idempotence, and monotonicity to characterize pooling through a continuous strictly increasing exposure transform. The higher-dimensional appendix replaces scalar monotonicity with a cyclic-monotonicity condition tied to gradients of convex functions.

key_findings.claim: The logarithmic score is a central example of QA pooling but is excluded from the stated online regret theorem because it is unbounded.
key_findings.evidence: Logarithmic pooling is derived as a headline special case, while Theorem 5.3 explicitly assumes bounded scoring and obtains a finite global exposure bound. Thus the general pooling definition includes log score, but the advertised adversarial O(sqrt(T)) learning guarantee does not automatically cover it.

method.core_idea: Map probabilities through the exposure function of the same proper scoring rule used for evaluation, average in that dual space, and map the result back to a coherent forecast.
method.mechanism: Use the Savage representation of proper scores through a strictly convex expected-reward function G, express score gaps as Bregman divergences, define the aggregate by a weighted exposure subgradient, prove max-min optimality with convex geometry and KKT conditions, establish weight-score concavity, apply online gradient descent, and characterize the operator through aggregation axioms.
assumptions: Experts report coherent distributions over a finite outcome set and lie in the score's finite forecast domain.
The scoring rule is regular, continuous, and strictly proper under the paper's convention.
Convex exposure is required for the concavity, online-learning, and broad axiomatization results, though not for max-min optimality.
The online regret theorem additionally requires a bounded score and hence a bounded exposure norm.
The online comparator is the best fixed weight vector over the observed horizon.
The subcontracting interpretation uses the same score for the agent and proportional payments to experts.

techniques.role: Represents a proper scoring rule with a convex expected-reward function and its exposure gradient.
Expresses QA pooling as minimization of weighted scoring regret to expert forecasts.
Shows the pooled report equalizes and maximizes worst-case subcontracting profit.
Unifies linear and logarithmic pooling as different scoring-rule geometries.
Learns fixed expert weights with an adversarial square-root regret guarantee.
Recovers QA pooling from consistency, symmetry, continuity, and monotonicity-style properties.

evaluations.result: The QA pool is the unique maximizer and gives nonnegative worst-case profit
evaluations.baseline: Any alternative report under the same scoring contract

evaluations.setting: Adversarial sequence of expert forecasts and outcomes
evaluations.result: Online gradient descent achieves at most 3 sqrt(m) M sqrt(T) regret
evaluations.baseline: Best fixed QA-pool weight vector in hindsight

evaluations.result: QA pooling recovers weighted linear and normalized logarithmic pools respectively
evaluations.baseline: Using one fixed pool independently of the evaluation score

evaluations.result: The six stated axioms are necessary and sufficient for a QA transform

evaluations.metric: Calibration, sharpness, log loss, Brier score, or runtime
evaluations.baseline: No real-data pooling benchmark is reported

limitations: The no-regret theorem excludes unbounded proper scores such as the logarithmic score without further restrictions.
Convex exposure restricts the multiclass scoring rules covered by the weight-concavity and online-learning results.
The analysis uses finite outcome spaces and coherent expert distributions.
The comparator is a single fixed weight vector and cannot track nonstationary expert skill.
No empirical study compares calibration, accuracy, robustness, or computation with standard pools on real forecasts.
The theory does not model dependence among experts, shared information, strategic reporting, or latent information structures.
The max-min profit interpretation assumes aligned scoring contracts and exact proportional expert payments.
failure_modes: The scoring rule used to construct the pool differs from the rule used to evaluate or pay the aggregate.
Experts place boundary-zero probabilities under log score, making exposures or payments infinite.
Strongly correlated experts are treated as independent evidence and receive excessive aggregate influence.
Expert quality drifts, so the best fixed mixture is an inadequate online target.
A multiclass score lacks convex exposure, invalidating weight-score concavity.
Strategic experts adapt reports to the aggregation rule, while the proof treats submitted forecasts as fixed inputs.
Numerical inversion of the exposure map is ill-conditioned near the simplex boundary.
reusable_insights: Choose aggregation geometry and evaluation score jointly rather than defaulting to arithmetic averaging.
View forecast pools as Bregman barycenters to expose their implicit notion of disagreement.
Compare an online aggregator against the best mixture, not only the best individual expert.
Check boundedness and exposure geometry before transferring a regret theorem between scoring rules.
Use outcome-wise profit equalization as a diagnostic for robust pooling contracts.
Separate axiomatic coherence from empirical superiority; both need independent validation.
open_questions: Can logarithmic QA pooling obtain useful regret bounds under probability clipping or data-dependent local norms?
How should QA weights adapt under nonstationarity while retaining a meaningful mixture comparator?
Can expert dependence and shared evidence be incorporated without losing max-min optimality?
Which multiclass proper scores fail convex exposure, and can their induced pools still be learned efficiently?
How do QA pools compare empirically on calibration, sharpness, tail risk, and robustness across domains?
Can strategic incentive compatibility be combined with parallel QA aggregation?
What approximation guarantees are available when exposure inversion is solved numerically?

competitive_landscape.title: A Characterization of Scoring Rules for Linear Properties
competitive_landscape.difference: Abernethy and Frongillo characterize scoring rules eliciting linear properties through convex analysis and Bregman structure. The reviewed paper turns a proper score's exposure geometry into an explicit expert-pooling operator with max-min and online-weight results.

competitive_landscape.title: Online Aggregation of Probability Forecasts with Confidence
competitive_landscape.difference: V'yugin and Trunov study online probability forecasting with expert confidence and mixability, including CRPS-oriented guarantees. The reviewed paper learns weights specifically for the QA pool induced by the evaluation score and compares against the best fixed mixture.

competitive_landscape.title: Online Learning with Continuous Ranked Probability Score
competitive_landscape.difference: V'yugin and Trunov derive online aggregation guarantees for probability forecasts evaluated by CRPS. The reviewed paper gives a general proper-scoring-rule construction under convex exposure and targets the best weighted QA mixture rather than one CRPS-specific combination protocol.

competitive_landscape.title: A Second-order Bound with Excess Losses
competitive_landscape.difference: Gaillard, Stoltz, and van Erven obtain second-order expert-advice regret bounds driven by excess losses. Their standard comparator is expert-oriented, whereas the reviewed result exploits QA weight concavity to compete with the best fixed pooled forecast weights.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Proper scoring rules canonically induce QA pooling, which uniquely maximizes worst-case subcontracting profit, admits no-regret weight learning under bounded convex exposure, and is characterized by natural pooling axioms.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper supplies a Bregman/exposure definition, Theorems 4.1 and 5.1-5.3, binary and multidimensional characterizations, and familiar linear and logarithmic special cases.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest novelty is the unification of scoring, pooling, max-min contracts, and learning expert weights in one geometry. The contribution is theoretical; operational value still depends on handling unbounded scores, dependence, drift, strategic behavior, and empirical performance.
